newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhs seen to move to stable, liberal economy.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhs seen to move to stable, liberal economy.

text.p: The head of Kazakhstan's new political and economic think-tank said on Wednesday he saw the future of the vast oil-rich Central Asian state as a liberal growing economy bridging Europe and Asia.
"The task is to make the economy even more liberal than in Europe and Asia," Yerzhan Utembayev, chairman of the Agency for Strategic Planning, told his first news conference.
"Kazakhstan must become a country bridging Europe and Asia," he said.

The agency, set up last month and reporting directly to the Kazakh president, will handle the former Soviet republic's long-term economic and geopolitical planning. It will also work out annual plans for ministries.

Utembayev said Kazakhstan -- a vast steppe five times larger than Franch sprawling across Europe and Asia -- badly needed economic revival to perform its political role as a bridge between East and West.
And he said the economy was likely to rebound further this year, with a 1.0-1.5 percent growth of gross domestic product after a moderate 0.5 percent growth last year.
Output had been shrinking rapidly since 1991.
"There is a general feeling that the worst is over now," John Nellis, senior manager in charge of the World Bank's enterprise reform and privatisation department, told a news conference later.
Utembayev said he expected that by the year 2000 the economy would start growing by 4-5 percent a year.
He said inflation was forecast to drop by the beginning of the next century to 3-5 percent a year from 28.7 percent last year and 17 percent targeted for this year.
"We view these as eminently achievable targets," Nellis, visiting Kazakhstan, told Reuters after the news conference.
Foreign investment remains crucial for a sustained economic growth, and Utembayev said foreign investors were likely to invest in Kazakhstan this year alone $1.0-1.5 billion.
Officials said earlier that direct foreign investment had reached $3.5 billion by the beginning of this year.
"Most of the investment has been made so far in the promising oil and gas sector but we hope that foreigners will start investing in less attractive branches as well," Utembayev said.
